newsitem.title: USA: Manufacturing index rises in December; markets skid.
newsitem.headline: Manufacturing index rises in December; markets skid.

text.p: A widely watched index of manufacturing activity rose in December, the nation's purchasing managers said Thursday, sending a shiver through financial markets and driving stock and bond prices lower.

The National Association of Purchasing Management said its index of maufacturing activity rose to 54.0 in December, the highest in six months, from 52.7 in November. A reading above 50 points to growth in manufacturing, while one below that level indicates contraction.

"The manufacturing sector grew more rapidly in December than in November with new orders indicating faster rates of growth and prices moving upward," Norbert Ore, who heads the group's monthly survey, said in a statement.

The report, the first broad glimpse at the economy each month, was also the first major indicator of the new year and had been widely awaited in financial markets. Private economists had expected a reading of 51.5 for December.

The latest reading pointed to a possible pickup in economic growth that could lead to accelerating inflation and higher interest rates, traders and analysts said. The group's index stood at 54.3 in June.

The purchasing group said its index of prices paid rose to 51.5 last month from 45.9 in November, indicating rising prices after two months of declines. It was the highest reading since July 1995, when the index was 59.
So far, most price increases have been absorbed by manufacturers and retailers and not passed on, helping keep consumer price inflation tame.
But bond market investors, keenly sensitive to any signs of possible inflation, sent prices tumbling after the report. Inflation erodes the returns on their long-term investments.

The drop in bonds helped drive stocks lower, and the Dow Jones industrial average lost 45 points to 6,403 in late morning trading after falling as much as 95 points earlier. Stock investors were nervous after Tuesday's slide of 101 points in the 30-share Dow average.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 1-9/32, or $12.81 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.75 percent from 6.64 percent on Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in the opposite direction.
The nation's financial markets were closed on Wednesday for New Year's Day.

In its report, the purchasors group said that 13 percent of purchasing managers reported paying higher prices in December, 13 percent reported paying lower prices and 74 percent said prices were unchanged from November.
The group's members buy goods ranging from cardboard to computer chips and other finished and raw materials for the nation's major corporations.
